title: Air Through a Gap: F, V, and TH
label: Lesson 03

goal.html: Today's goal: Make four sounds that Korean doesn't have: /f v θ ð/. The air must keep flowing. Blocking the air turns them into ㅍ, ㅂ, ㅆ, ㄷ.
By the end, coffee no longer sounds like copy, very not like berry, and think not like sink.

blocks.html: Marks: ● strong beat · · weak beat · CAPITALS = stressed · | = small pause · ‿ = link. Full key in Lesson 01.
01 / Understand the pattern
1. Stops vs. flowing sounds

In Lesson 02, the air stopped completely (/p b t d k ɡ/). Today's sounds are fricatives: the air never stops. It squeezes through a narrow gap and makes friction noise. You should be able to hold each one for as long as you have breath: ffffff, vvvvvv, θθθθθθ.
Why this is hard: Korean has no sounds made with the teeth on the lip or the tongue at the teeth. So Korean replaces them with the nearest stop:
f → ㅍ · v → ㅂ · θ → ㅆ (or ㄸ) · ð → ㄷ
Each replacement stops the air. To an English listener, that is usually a different word.
Test: Can you hold the sound for three seconds? If yes, it's a fricative. You can't hold ㅍ or ㅂ.

blocks.text: 2. /f/ and /v/: top teeth on the lower lip
blocks.html: 2. /f/ and /v/: top teeth on the lower lip
Rest your upper teeth lightly on your lower lip. Blow air through the gap: that's /f/. Add your voice (throat buzz): that's /v/.
Do not close both lips. Closing both lips makes /p/ or /b/.

rows.html: Top teeth on lower lip, air flows
Top teeth on lower lip, air flows

blocks.alt: /f v/: top teeth on the lower lip, air keeps flowing. ㅍ (/p/): both lips close and the air stops. Top: side view. Bottom: front view.

blocks.html: 3. /θ/ and /ð/: tongue at the teeth
Put your tongue tip lightly against the back of your upper teeth (or just between the teeth). Blow air over it: that's /θ/ as in think. Add voice: that's /ð/ as in this.
You don't need to bite hard or stick your tongue far out. A gentle touch is enough, but the air must keep moving.

rows.html: Tongue tip at upper teeth, air flows
Tongue tip at upper teeth, air flows

blocks.html: The spelling th doesn't tell you which one it is. Think, three, thank have /θ/. This, they, the have /ð/.

blocks.alt: /θ ð/: tongue tip at the teeth, air keeps flowing. ㅆ (/s/): the tongue hides behind the teeth. Top: side view. Bottom: front view.

blocks.html: 4. What a listener hears
If you use the Korean replacement, an English listener often hears a different word:

blocks.text: 5. The most common TH words are small and weak
blocks.html: 5. The most common TH words are small and weak

The most frequent /ð/ words are function words: the, this, that, they, them, their, there, than, then. In sentences they are usually weak (·): short and quiet. Keep them quick, but keep the tongue at the teeth. A light /ð/ is fine; a ㄷ is not.
the = /ðə/ before a consonant sound (the book), /ði/ before a vowel sound (the apple).

blocks.text: I. Hard clusters: still one beat
blocks.html: I. Hard clusters: still one beat
Korean splits these into 3–4 beats. They are one beat each.
Fifth, months, and clothes are hard for native speakers too. Many Americans say months as "munce" and clothes as "cloze." Those simplified forms are normal.

The CAPITALS land on the claps. Each the, them, their, than is squeezed in between. Keep the tongue at the teeth, but make it fast.
Two opposite mistakes:

items: Making small TH words too strong: GIVE THEM THEIR COATS (● ● ● ●) sounds angry or robotic.
Turning them into ㄷ to save time: GIVE dem dare COATS.

Short reading: Thursday's Walk
Goal: Keep the air flowing on every f, v, and th, while keeping the rhythm light on small words.
Focus: Read the passage once and mark the strong beats and pauses yourself. Then open the marked version to check, and read again while tapping.

On Thursday, three friends visited a village by a river. Their guide, Vivian, showed them a narrow path through the trees. The weather was warm, and all three soon felt thirsty. They stopped at a small shop and bought fresh fruit and water. Vivian told them that her father had built the wooden bridge ahead. The friends thanked her for the visit and walked across together. From the other side, they could see five white birds above the river and a field full of flowers.

05 / Check yourself

items: What do /v/ and /b/ do differently with the lips?
Do Thursday and their begin with the same TH sound?
If you say think as 씽크, what word might a listener hear?
What is the quick test for a fricative?
In GIVE them their COATS, which words are weak?
How many beats are in three and friend? How many are in 쓰리 and 프렌드?
/v/: top teeth on the lower lip, air flows. /b/: both lips close, air stops.
You can hold it: ffff, vvvv, θθθθ. You can't hold a stop like ㅍ or ㅂ.
them and their. They are quick and light, but still /ð/.
One each. 쓰리 has two; 프렌드 has three.

keep the, them, their light and quick without turning them into ㄷ
